questions.prompt: Northbridge Retail's point-of-sale application tries to write directly to the network interface card's hardware registers instead of asking the operating system to send the data. Per the three-layer model from this lesson, what's wrong with that?
options: Nothing is wrong — applications are expected to talk to hardware directly whenever it improves performance

Applications are software that runs through the operating system, never talking to hardware directly — the OS exists specifically to mediate device access so one misbehaving program can't control hardware on its own
This is only a problem on Windows, not Linux, because Linux lets applications bypass the OS freely
The CPU would reject the instruction, but RAM and storage would still accept it without issue
questions.explain: The lesson's three-layer model is explicit: an application is software that runs through the operating system, never talking to hardware directly. The OS's job of giving programs a consistent way to access devices and files, without each program needing to know the exact hardware details underneath, is exactly what a direct hardware write like this would bypass.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when RAM runs short, one option the operating system has is to move some memory out to a slower disk location instead of terminating a process outright — this is called ________.
questions.explain: The lesson describes the OS's response to memory pressure as a choice: slow things down by swapping some memory out to disk (far slower than RAM), or in more extreme cases, start terminating processes to free up space.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually means, per the servers-vs-clients lesson.
right: An operating system build tuned to run unattended, answering many clients reliably
Whatever initiates a request for something — a role, not a specific device
Whatever receives a request and sends back a response — a role, not a specific device
The basic back-and-forth pattern nearly all client-server communication follows
questions.explain: Client and server are roles in a conversation, not fixed categories of hardware: a client initiates a request, a server receives it and responds. That request/response pattern is the basic shape nearly all client-server communication follows, and a server edition OS is simply a build tuned to answer many such requests unattended and reliably.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about virtual machines and hypervisors, per this lesson.
options: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on physical hardware with no underlying host OS, which is why data centers and the cloud use it
A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on top of a regular host operating system, common on developer laptops
A VM's guest operating system can tell it isn't running on real, dedicated hardware, and must be specially written to account for this
Virtualization exists mainly to make a single application run faster than it would on dedicated hardware
One physical server running a hypervisor can host several isolated VMs, each sized to what its own workload actually needs
questions.explain: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware with no host OS, which is why they're the data-center/cloud standard; Type 2 hypervisors run as an application on a host OS, common for laptops and testing. A guest OS is convincingly fooled — it behaves exactly as if it had dedicated hardware and is unaware it doesn't. Virtualization exists to stop paying for idle hardware by letting one physical server host several isolated, appropriately-sized VMs — it's about utilization, not making any one application run faster.

questions.prompt: Match each networking term to its definition or Northbridge Retail example, per this lesson.
right: The global mesh of interconnected networks using common protocols
A small chunk of data, with header information, that a message is broken into for transmission
A connection between two separate LANs, such as the link between Northbridge's warehouse and corporate office
A network confined to one site, owned and controlled entirely by one organization, like Northbridge's warehouse network
questions.explain: Data crosses a network in packets, not one continuous stream. Northbridge's warehouse network is a LAN (one site, one owner); the link to its corporate office is a WAN (a connection between two LANs); and the public internet is simply the largest WAN of all, a global mesh of networks agreeing to forward each other's traffic.

questions.prompt: A cashier's register at Northbridge Retail can reach every other device on its own local network just fine, but any connection beyond the local router times out. Per this lesson's layer-by-layer troubleshooting shortcut, which OSI layer does this symptom point to first?
options: Physical
Data Link
Network
Transport
Session
Application
questions.explain: The lesson's troubleshooting shortcut is explicit: 'Local traffic works but anything beyond the local router fails? That's network layer — check IP addressing and routing.' Everything within the local network already works, which rules out the layers below Network; the failure begins specifically at crossing the router.
questions.distractorExplain: Data Link (option B) would be the answer if the device couldn't find anything on the local network at all — but here local traffic works perfectly fine, which rules Data Link out. The symptom only appears once traffic needs to go beyond the local router, which is exactly the Network layer's job of routing across different networks.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when a device on Northbridge's warehouse LAN with a private address needs to reach something on the public internet, the router performs ________, swapping the private source address for a public one.
questions.explain: Private addresses are never routed on the public internet. When a device needs to reach the outside, the router performs Network Address Translation (NAT), swapping the private source address for one globally unique, routable public address.

questions.prompt: Northbridge's warehouse subnet is 192.168.10.0/26, and the next subnet for the corporate office starts cleanly at 192.168.10.64/26. What is the corporate office subnet's broadcast address?
questions.explain: A /26 leaves 6 host bits, so each block spans 64 addresses. The office block runs from 192.168.10.64 (network address) through 192.168.10.127. The broadcast address is always the last address in the block, with every host bit set to 1 — that's 192.168.10.127, not .126 (the last usable host) or .63 (the warehouse subnet's own broadcast address one block earlier).

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a packet's journey off its own subnet in the order this lesson describes, starting from a laptop on Northbridge's corporate office subnet sending data to the cloud-hosted order database.
items: The laptop checks whether the destination IP is on its own subnet, finds it isn't, and sends the packet to its default gateway
The router receives the packet and checks its routing table for the best match to the destination
If the destination is another of Northbridge's own subnets, the router forwards it directly there
If the destination is out on the internet instead, the router forwards it toward its default route and the packet keeps hopping through other routers until it arrives
questions.explain: Every hop repeats the same pattern: check the destination, look it up, forward one step closer. The laptop first recognizes the destination isn't local and hands off to its default gateway (the router), which checks its routing table and either forwards directly to another known subnet or falls back to its default route out toward the internet.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of resolving northbridgeretail.com in the order a DNS lookup actually travels through, per this lesson.
items: The stub resolver on the shopper's laptop checks its own local cache first
If there's no cached answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver run by the ISP or a public service
The recursive resolver asks a root server where to find .com, then asks the .com TLD server where to find northbridgeretail.com
The TLD server points to Northbridge Retail's authoritative name server, which holds the real records and returns the actual IP address
questions.explain: A DNS lookup passes through several hands: the stub resolver's own cache first, then a recursive resolver that does the legwork, which queries root and TLD servers for direction, which finally point to the authoritative name server holding the real answer.

questions.prompt: What does a DHCP server actually do for a device joining Northbridge Retail's network?
options: It automatically hands the device an IP address from a managed pool, along with settings like the subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server, through the Discover/Offer/Request/Acknowledge exchange
It manually assigns a permanent, unchanging IP address that an administrator must type in for every new device
It translates the device's private IP address into a public one so it can reach the internet
It encrypts all traffic the device sends until it reaches its destination
It forwards the device's DNS queries to a recursive resolver and caches the answers
It scans the device for open ports and reports which services are listening
questions.explain: A DHCP server hands out an address from a pool it manages, along with the subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server a device should use, through the four-message DORA exchange: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes NAT, from the IP addressing lesson, not DHCP. DHCP's job is assigning an address and settings automatically to a device joining the network; it's NAT that later translates that device's private address into a public one for internet access. The two often run on the same router, which is exactly why they're easy to mix up, but they solve two different problems.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about TCP and UDP, per this lesson.
options: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before any data moves
UDP guarantees packets arrive in the correct order, just without retransmitting any that get lost

Northbridge's live warehouse dashboard uses UDP because losing an occasional update doesn't matter, and waiting for TCP's handshake and retransmission logic on every update would add more delay than it's worth
A checkout page uses TCP because a dropped or scrambled packet during checkout is a lost order, not an acceptable loss
TCP and UDP are both connection-based protocols that each require a handshake before sending any data
questions.explain: TCP opens with a three-way handshake and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery, which is exactly why checkout and anything involving money runs on it. UDP throws out the handshake, acknowledgments, and guaranteed ordering entirely — it has no ordering guarantee at all, not just no retransmission — which is why it suits time-sensitive, loss-tolerant traffic like the warehouse dashboard. UDP is connectionless, so it never performs a handshake.

questions.code:
$ curl -i https://northbridgeretail.com/checkout
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
questions.prompt: This curl request to /checkout comes back with a 500 status code. What does that specifically indicate, per this lesson's status code table?
options: The server itself hit an error trying to handle a request it did receive
The requested path doesn't exist on an otherwise-working server
The request succeeded normally
The client should look somewhere else instead, such as a redirected URL
questions.explain: Per the lesson's status code table, 500 means the server itself hit an error trying to handle the request — distinct from 404 (nothing exists at that path), 200 (success), or 301/302 (look somewhere else instead).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a certificate's issuer is a ________ — a trusted organization whose entire job is verifying that whoever requested the certificate actually controls that domain before signing off on it.
questions.explain: A certificate contains the domain, an expiration date, a public key, and an issuer — a Certificate Authority (CA) that verifies domain ownership before signing. Browsers trust a certificate only if it was signed by a CA they already recognize.

questions.prompt: A laptop at Northbridge Retail can browse the web through the office firewall with just a single 'allow outbound HTTPS' rule configured — there's no matching inbound rule for the responses that come back. Why does this work?
options: The firewall is stateful, so once it allows an outbound connection, it automatically allows the matching return traffic without needing a separate rule
HTTPS traffic is exempt from firewall rules entirely
The firewall is stateless, so it doesn't track connections at all and simply allows everything by default
The response traffic is actually a separate new outbound connection initiated by the laptop
questions.explain: Most modern firewalls are stateful: once a rule allows an outbound connection, the firewall automatically allows the matching return traffic. An older stateless firewall would need explicit rules for both directions of every conversation.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Northbridge's router is configured so any inbound connection to the public IP on UDP port 51820 is always forwarded to the VPN gateway's private address — a manual, permanent entry in the translation table rather than a temporary automatic one. This is called ________.
questions.explain: Port forwarding creates a permanent, manual entry in NAT's translation table so a specific port is deliberately punched through, while everything else on the public IP still has no mapping and gets dropped.

questions.prompt: Match each load-balancing term to what it actually does, per this lesson.
right: Routes a given client's requests to the same backend server each time
Cycles through backend servers in order, one request each
A periodic request used to confirm a backend server is actually working
Sends the next request to whichever backend server has the fewest active connections
questions.explain: Round robin cycles through servers in order; least connections sends the next request to whichever server has the fewest active connections; IP hash keeps a given client's requests on the same server; and a health check is the periodic probe that keeps the load balancer from sending traffic to a server that's actually down.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about VPNs and bastion hosts, per this lesson.
options: A site-to-site VPN permanently connects two entire networks, such as Northbridge's office and its cloud VPC, with no action required from any individual user
A remote-access VPN connects one person's device to a private network on demand
A bastion host is the only machine allowed to initiate SSH or RDP connections into a private subnet, rather than every server having its own exposed management port
Once traffic is inside a VPN tunnel, firewall and security-group rules no longer apply to it
A bastion host replaces the need for any security-group rules on the servers it connects to
questions.explain: Site-to-site VPNs permanently connect two networks; remote-access VPNs connect one device to a network on demand. A bastion host is the single hardened entry point for administrative access. Neither tool replaces the firewall and security-group rules covered earlier in the chapter — a security group still only allows inbound traffic from the bastion's address, and the bastion itself still only accepts connections from the VPN's range. Each layer narrows the next one down further, rather than any layer making the others unnecessary.

questions.code:
$ ping checkout.northbridgeretail.com
64 bytes from 203.0.113.42: icmp_seq=1 ttl=58 time=11.2 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.42: icmp_seq=2 ttl=58 time=10.8 ms
questions.prompt: This ping to checkout.northbridgeretail.com succeeds with fast reply times, but the checkout page itself fails to load in a browser. What does the successful ping actually prove, per this lesson?
options: The network path is up and that specific host responds to ICMP — nothing about whether the web application behind it is actually working
The checkout application itself is functioning correctly
DNS has resolved the name to the correct address
The TLS certificate for the site is valid
questions.explain: ping answers one narrow question — is this address reachable, and roughly how fast — and nothing more. A server can ping just fine while its checkout process is completely broken; proving the application works requires a tool like curl aimed at the application itself.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if `ss` on the checkout server shows nothing listening on port 443 like this, no firewall rule or load balancer configuration will ever make the service reachable, because the real problem is that nothing is ________ on that port.
questions.explain: ss and netstat answer which ports a server is actually listening on. If nothing is listening on 443, no firewall rule or load balancer configuration downstream of that will ever make the service reachable — the application itself isn't bound to the port at all.

questions.prompt: Put these layers in the bottom-up order this lesson recommends checking when Northbridge Retail's checkout page reports an error.
items: Physical / network reachability — is the host even reachable?
DNS — does the name resolve to the address expected?
Transport / port — is something actually listening on the expected port?
Application — only now dig into application logs and behavior
questions.explain: Working up the stack instead of guessing at the top narrows problems fastest: confirm reachability, then DNS, then that the right port is actually listening, and only once those layers are confirmed working does it make sense to dig into application logs.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four failure scenarios covered in this lesson.
options: A certificate that expires overnight causes a browser security warning even though ping still succeeds and nothing was deployed or changed
Stale DNS after a migration happens because some resolvers are still serving an old cached answer, usually because the TTL wasn't lowered before the change
An overloaded backend during a traffic spike typically makes both ping and DNS fail along with the application
A firewall rule blocking the load balancer's own health-check traffic can get every backend marked unhealthy even though ping and curl from inside the network still work fine
`ss` showing abnormal connection counts on backend servers is the clue that confirms an overloaded backend, rather than a misconfiguration
questions.explain: An expired certificate fails TLS validation specifically, with ping and the server otherwise healthy. Stale DNS is a caching problem traceable to a TTL that wasn't lowered in advance. A misconfigured firewall rule can block health-check traffic specifically, while basic connectivity still works. An overloaded backend's signature is intermittent failures with ping and DNS both still succeeding — the service exists and mostly works, it just can't keep up — and ss showing abnormal connection counts is exactly what confirms that's a capacity problem, not a misconfiguration.

questions.prompt: A hosting provider lets Northbridge Retail rent servers, but provisioning any new capacity requires a phone call and can take several days to actually show up. Which of the five NIST cloud characteristics is this provider clearly missing?
options: On-demand self-service
Broad network access
Resource pooling
Measured service
questions.explain: On-demand self-service means a user provisions resources themselves, through a console or API, without calling anyone. A provider that requires a phone call and a multi-day wait to provision capacity is missing exactly that characteristic, even if it offers the other four.

questions.prompt: Match each cloud service model to its description and the matching Northbridge Retail example from this lesson.
right: The provider manages everything including the application itself — Northbridge's email and CRM running on Microsoft 365 and Salesforce
The provider hands you raw compute, storage, and networking and you manage the OS up — Northbridge's custom checkout VMs
The provider also manages the OS and runtime and you just deploy code — Northbridge's marketing website
questions.explain: IaaS hands you raw VMs, storage, and networking that you manage yourself, like Northbridge's checkout VMs. PaaS also manages the OS and runtime so you just deploy code, like their marketing website. SaaS manages everything including the application, like their Microsoft 365 and Salesforce subscriptions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about regions, availability zones, and region pairs, per this lesson.
options: An availability zone is a physically separate data center within a region, with independent power and cooling but low-latency links to the others
Deploying across multiple availability zones in the same region protects against a whole-region disaster the same way a region pair does
Region pairs are geographically distant from each other specifically so replicating across both protects against a true regional disaster
Placing a resource physically close to its users reduces latency, which is why providers offer dozens of regions worldwide
A small internal tool with no uptime requirements gains nothing from considering region or zone placement, so multi-region deployment should be the default for every workload regardless of cost
questions.explain: An availability zone protects against a local failure (one data center going down); it does not protect against a true regional disaster the way a geographically distant region pair does. Proximity to users reduces latency, which is why providers offer many regions. The lesson explicitly says more regions and zones mean more cost and complexity, and a small internal tool might run fine in a single zone — multi-region is a tradeoff decision, not a default for every workload.

questions.prompt: An employee at Northbridge Retail leaves a cloud storage container open to the public internet, and customer data leaks as a result. Under the shared responsibility model, whose failure is this, and why?
options: Northbridge Retail's — data classification and access control are always the customer's responsibility, regardless of which service model (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS) is in use
The cloud provider's — the provider is responsible for every resource a customer creates, including how it's configured
Nobody's — a publicly open storage container is a normal, secure default configuration
Northbridge Retail's provider, because the shared responsibility model only applies to IaaS workloads
questions.explain: The customer is always responsible for their own data, identities, and access control, no matter which service model they use. Study after study of real cloud incidents finds the provider's infrastructure almost never failed — what failed was a customer-side setting, exactly like a storage container left open to the public internet.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Northbridge's checkout VMs run continuously all year, so the team commits to using them for a full year in exchange for a significant discount. This pricing model is called ________ capacity.
questions.explain: Reserved capacity means committing to a resource for one or three years in exchange for a significant discount, well suited to workloads known to run continuously — unlike pay-as-you-go (no commitment, most flexible) or spot (unused capacity, reclaimable with little notice).

questions.prompt: The new distribution office needs to support roughly 50 devices today, with some room to grow. Which CIDR block does the capstone's own addressing plan actually use for this office subnet?
options: /26 (62 usable addresses)
/27 (30 usable addresses)
/24 (254 usable addresses)
/30 (2 usable addresses)
questions.explain: The capstone's addressing plan uses 10.20.4.0/26, giving 62 usable addresses — comfortably covering roughly 50 devices with room to grow, without wasting as much address space as a full /24 would. A /27's 30 usable addresses would already be too tight.

questions.code:
$ ping 10.20.1.5        # VPN gateway
64 bytes from 10.20.1.5: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.1 ms

$ ping 10.40.2.10       # cloud-hosted inventory system, via VPN
Request timeout for icmp_seq 0
questions.prompt: In the capstone's broken scenario, a teammate insists 'the VPN is up,' and indeed a ping to the VPN gateway succeeds, as shown above. So what was actually blocking the office from reaching the cloud-hosted inventory system?
options: An outbound firewall rule at the office's edge allowed traffic to the checkout service's IP range but was never updated to also include the inventory system's IP range
The VPN tunnel itself was down despite what the teammate claimed
DNS at the office was resolving the inventory system's name to the wrong address
The inventory system's own TLS certificate had expired
questions.explain: The VPN tunnel being up only guarantees connectivity through the tunnel itself, not that traffic is actually allowed to pass through it. The real fault was a separate, independent control: an outbound firewall rule written for an earlier deadline that covered the checkout service's IP range but was never updated when the inventory system was added later.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: besides an architecture diagram, a README, and the problem/fix narrative, a strong capstone writeup needs a way to ________ that the fix actually worked, not just a claim that it did.
questions.explain: A portfolio-ready writeup needs a specific test — a ping, a curl, a traceroute — that proves the fix actually worked, not just an assertion that it did. Verification is what separates a credible writeup from an unsubstantiated one.
